title: A Lunch Pail on the School Desk
subtheme: A Lunch Pail on the School Desk
description: An older-style lunch container waits beside a classroom desk.
cardDescription: An older-style lunch container waits beside a classroom desk.
focus: The setting is a Lunch Pail on the School Desk. Match each clue to a thing, action, or description in that scene.
solvingTip: Begin with a short answer you recognize. Use its crossing letters to work toward the longer scene words.
words: Food made with filling between pieces of bread
Round tree fruit with a core
Cloth or paper square used at a meal
Part held when carrying or using something
Material such as iron or copper

answerNotes.SANDWICH: A sandwich places a filling between pieces of bread. An open-faced version uses just one supporting slice.
answerNotes.APPLE: An apple has a peel, flesh, and a seed-bearing core. Cider is made by pressing apples for their juice.
answerNotes.MILK: Milk is a dairy liquid used in drinks and batters. Cream is the richer portion, with a higher fat content.
answerNotes.SCHOOL: School memories vary between generations. These scenes select familiar older objects without assuming every reader used the same equipment.
answerNotes.HANDLE: A handle is the part made for the hand to grip. Its shape depends on whether the object is carried, pulled, poured, or turned.
answerNotes.LID: A lid is a removable cover. On a cooking pot it helps contain heat and steam; on a jar it closes the opening.
answerNotes.METAL: Metal names a family of materials including iron, copper, and aluminum. The word does not identify which metal a particular tool contains.
answerNotes.COOKIE: American English uses cookie for a small sweet baked treat. In Britain, many such treats are called biscuits.
answerNotes.BAG: A bag is a flexible carrying container. A pocket is generally a smaller compartment attached to clothing or another bag.

title: Writing with Chalk at the Blackboard
subtheme: Writing with Chalk at the Blackboard
description: A soft white stick leaves lesson words on a dark classroom board.
cardDescription: A soft white stick leaves lesson words on a dark classroom board.
focus: The setting is writing with Chalk at the Blackboard. Match each clue to a thing, action, or description in that scene.
solvingTip: Begin with a short answer you recognize. Use its crossing letters to work toward the longer scene words.
words: Soft white stick for writing on a board
Dark classroom surface written on with chalk
Unit of teaching prepared for a class

answerNotes.CHALK: Chalk leaves a powdery mark that can be wiped away. It is useful on a board or pavement but does not behave like permanent ink.
answerNotes.BLACKBOARD: A blackboard is a writing surface used with chalk. Boards can be dark green as well as black despite the traditional name.
answerNotes.WHITE: White is a color description, not a flower or bird name. Crossings can help when a clue asks for a color rather than a species.
answerNotes.ERASER: An eraser removes many graphite marks by rubbing them from the paper. It does not work the same way on every kind of ink.
answerNotes.TEACHER: A teacher guides learning. A class is the group of learners or the lesson session, not the teacher's job title.
answerNotes.LETTER: Letter can mean a written message or one alphabet character. An envelope clue points to the message sense.
answerNotes.NUMBER: A number can count an amount or identify something. A telephone number identifies a connection rather than measuring its size.

description: Keep writing and drawing supplies together before lessons begin.
cardDescription: Keep writing and drawing supplies together before lessons begin.
focus: The setting is a Pencil Box Before Class. Match each clue to a thing, action, or description in that scene.
solvingTip: Begin with a short answer you recognize. Use its crossing letters to work toward the longer scene words.
words: Writing tool with a graphite core
Container with a base and sides
Tool used to rub out a written mistake
Straight measuring tool marked with units
Colored wax stick used for drawing
Small tool that forms a pencil point
Material used for writing or wrapping
Hue, such as red or blue

answerNotes.PENCIL: The writing core of a modern pencil is graphite, not metallic lead. Lead remains a traditional everyday name for it.
answerNotes.BOX: A box is a container rather than its contents. In a hobby clue, a kit may come in a box but the two words are not interchangeable.
answerNotes.ERASER: An eraser removes many graphite marks by rubbing them from the paper. It does not work the same way on every kind of ink.
answerNotes.PEN: A pen writes with ink. A pencil uses graphite, which can usually be removed with an eraser.
answerNotes.LID: A lid is a removable cover. On a cooking pot it helps contain heat and steam; on a jar it closes the opening.
answerNotes.SCHOOL: School memories vary between generations. These scenes select familiar older objects without assuming every reader used the same equipment.
answerNotes.PAPER: Paper can be folded, cut, and written on. Card stock is heavier and stiffer, making it useful for tags and greeting cards.
answerNotes.POINT: Point names a tapered end. A sharpened pencil needs a usable point, while a worn one makes a broader mark.
answerNotes.COLOR: Color names such as red, blue, and yellow describe appearance. They can help with a flower scene without requiring botanical vocabulary.

title: The School Bell at Recess
description: A ringing signal sends the class outside for play.
cardDescription: A ringing signal sends the class outside for play.
focus: The setting is the School Bell at Recess. Match each clue to a thing, action, or description in that scene.
solvingTip: Begin with a short answer you recognize. Use its crossing letters to work toward the longer scene words.
words: Metal object that rings when struck
Movable panel at a room's entrance
Hanging seat that moves back and forth

answerNotes.BELL: A bell rings when a clapper or striker vibrates it. A school bell and a decorative handbell use that same basic sound-making idea.
answerNotes.RECESS: Recess is a break in the school day. The word here concerns time for play rather than the end of the whole school term.
answerNotes.SCHOOL: School memories vary between generations. These scenes select familiar older objects without assuming every reader used the same equipment.
answerNotes.CLOCK: A clock shows time. The hour hand moves more slowly than the minute hand on a traditional clock face.
answerNotes.DOOR: A door is the movable panel at an entrance. Hinges let it swing, while a latch or lock holds it closed.
answerNotes.LINE: Line can mean a row, a drawn mark, or a fishing cord. The clue's action helps distinguish those meanings.
answerNotes.GAME: Game names the organized activity or contest. Equipment such as a bat or board is used in the game but is not the game itself.
answerNotes.SWING: Swing can name a hanging seat or the action of moving a bat. The porch and ballpark settings point to different meanings.

solvingTip: Begin with a short answer you recognize. Use its crossing letters to work toward the longer scene words.
words: Piece of stiff paper carrying a message
School worker who helps pupils learn
One part of the school year
To follow and understand written words
Make letters using a pencil or pen
Public board with words or symbols

answerNotes.REPORT: A school report summarizes progress. It may include several subjects rather than a single assignment's mark.
answerNotes.CARD: Card can mean a printed greeting or a playing piece. An envelope points to a greeting; a deck or suit points to a game.
answerNotes.GRADE: A grade records performance in schoolwork. Report cards can use letters, numbers, or written comments depending on the school.
answerNotes.SCHOOL: School memories vary between generations. These scenes select familiar older objects without assuming every reader used the same equipment.
answerNotes.TEACHER: A teacher guides learning. A class is the group of learners or the lesson session, not the teacher's job title.
answerNotes.NAME: A name identifies a person or thing. In a family album, adding names helps later readers recognize the people pictured.
answerNotes.TERM: A term is part of a school year. Its length depends on the school's calendar.
answerNotes.HOME: Home can mean a dwelling or the local side in a sporting match. Read the clue before applying the familiar household meaning.
answerNotes.SIGN: Sign can be a public notice or the action of writing a name. Check whether the clue describes an object or asks for a verb.
